intro: Two melodies and a two-bar drum rhythm survive an almost continuous crescendo. Ravel makes the changing instruments do the work that changing themes and keys usually do.
question: What changes when the melodies and rhythm barely change?

relations.label: The first tune changes instrument
relations.basis: The first melody is repeated by a new solo instrument before the second melody begins. This agrees with the listening notes’ flute statement and clarinet restatement near 13 and 56 s; chroma itself does not identify either instrument. CENS diagonal mean 0.935, sustained 45.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 45.5 s (cache/form/ravel-bolero.txt, candidate 52; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Two tunes, one crescendo
cues.text: Ravel repeats two melodies over a two-bar drum rhythm in three beats. Each melodic statement lasts eighteen bars. The growing orchestra supplies most of the large-scale change, while the repeated bass keeps the same tonal foundation.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the two-bar rhythm and eighteen-bar statement scheme. This is an overview of the piece, not a precisely timed drum entrance.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: First statement: flute
cues.text: The first melodic statement gives the opening tune to a flute. Listen across the phrase for its C-major notes above the repeated C-and-G foundation; the bass is not following every turn of the melody with a new harmony.
cues.evidence: Statement 1 is scored for flute. Its start is estimated around 0:13 from the opening changes around 0:12–0:18 and the eighteen-bar sequence; no aural check has been made.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second statement: clarinet
cues.text: The second statement repeats the first melody on clarinet. Compare this statement with the flute’s: the line is familiar, but a different instrument carries it.
cues.evidence: Statement 2 is scored for clarinet. Its start is estimated around 0:56 from the eighteen-bar sequence and a measured change around 0:54; the instrument comes from the score, not sound analysis.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Written for the ballet
cues.text: Boléro was conceived for Ida Rubinstein’s dance company and first staged in Paris in 1928. Its repeated rhythmic foundation belongs to a work originally made for dancers, before it became a concert-hall piece.
cues.evidence: Peter Laki’s Cleveland Orchestra programme note documents the commission and ballet origin: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/posts/ravels-bolero
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Third statement: bassoon
cues.text: The third statement introduces the second melody on bassoon, high in its range. This tune spans a wider range and includes flattened notes against the unchanged tonal foundation.
cues.evidence: Statement 3 introduces the second tune on bassoon. Its start is estimated around 1:44 from the eighteen-bar sequence and the level rise around 1:40–1:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fourth statement: small clarinet
cues.text: The fourth statement repeats the second tune on E♭ clarinet. Compare the same melodic contour with the bassoon’s earlier delivery; the smaller clarinet changes the colour, not the underlying pattern.
cues.evidence: Statement 4 is scored for E♭ clarinet. Its start is estimated around 2:28 from the eighteen-bar sequence and a change in spectral balance around 2:25–2:35.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fifth statement: oboe d’amore
cues.text: The fifth statement restores the first melody on oboe d’amore, pitched between oboe and cor anglais. The return of the tune and the change of instrument happen together within the repeated scheme.
cues.evidence: Statement 5 uses oboe d’amore. Its start is estimated around 3:10 from the eighteen-bar sequence and a change in spectral balance around 3:05–3:15.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sixth statement: blended colours
cues.text: The sixth statement combines muted trumpet with flute an octave above. Listen for the shared line as a composite colour rather than two competing solos.
cues.evidence: The score combines muted trumpet and flute in statement 6. Its start is estimated around 3:52 from the eighteen-bar sequence and the measured change around 3:50–3:55.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Seventh statement: tenor saxophone
cues.text: The seventh statement gives the second melody to tenor saxophone. Compare its long line with the bassoon and E♭ clarinet versions; the same phrase can occupy several instrumental identities.
cues.evidence: Statement 7 is the tenor saxophone statement. Its start is estimated around 4:42 from the eighteen-bar sequence and a level rise around 4:35–4:40.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Eighth statement: higher saxophones
cues.text: The eighth statement retains the second tune while moving the saxophone colour higher. Keep the long melodic phrase separate in your attention from the short repeated drum pattern.
cues.evidence: The score’s high saxophone parts belong to statement 8. Its start is estimated around 5:23 from the eighteen-bar sequence and a level change around 5:15–5:20; substitutions in this recording are not established.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ninth statement: composite tone
cues.text: The ninth statement combines horn, celesta and two piccolos on the first melody. Ravel distributes related upper pitches among separate instruments, making the scoring itself part of the tune’s changing colour.
cues.evidence: The score specifies this combination in statement 9. Its start is estimated around 6:02 from the eighteen-bar sequence and a level rise around 5:55–6:00.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tenth statement: grouped reeds
cues.text: The tenth statement combines oboe, oboe d’amore, cor anglais and clarinets. The succession of solo colours has become a succession of mixtures, while the first melody remains recognisable.
cues.evidence: The grouped reed scoring belongs to statement 10. Its start is estimated around 6:44 from the eighteen-bar sequence and changing spectral balance around 6:35–6:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Eleventh statement: trombone
cues.text: The eleventh statement gives the second melody to a solo trombone high in its range. Compare this brass version with the earlier woodwind statements over the same rhythmic foundation.
cues.evidence: Statement 11 is the score’s trombone solo. Its start is estimated around 7:27 from the eighteen-bar sequence and the level and spectral changes around 7:20–7:25.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Twelfth statement: winds together
cues.text: The twelfth statement repeats the second melody with a larger woodwind combination. The contrast is between one exposed melodic instrument and a group sharing the line, rather than between two different tunes.
cues.evidence: The score groups woodwinds in statement 12. Its start is estimated around 8:08 from the eighteen-bar sequence and a level increase around 8:00–8:05.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Thirteenth statement: violin melody
cues.text: The thirteenth statement brings first violins into the melodic foreground alongside winds. Until this stage, the strings have principally served the accompaniment; compare their new role with the opening solo colours.
cues.evidence: The score adds first violins to the tune in statement 13. Its start is estimated around 8:50 from the eighteen-bar sequence and changes around 8:40–8:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fourteenth statement: more strings
cues.text: The fourteenth statement adds second violins to the first in the melodic scoring. Doubling across registers broadens the line while preserving the familiar phrase.
cues.evidence: Statement 14 adds second violins in the score. Its start is estimated around 9:30 from the eighteen-bar sequence and a level and spectral change around 9:20–9:25.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Factories rather than taverns
cues.text: In a 1932 interview with the London Evening Standard, Ravel connected Boléro with his fascination for factory machinery. He wanted a vast factory in the background of a staging, rather than treating the original tavern setting as the only possibility.
cues.evidence: Peter Laki’s Cleveland Orchestra note quotes and identifies the 1932 interview: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/posts/ravels-bolero
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Fifteenth statement: retain the bass
cues.text: Through the fifteenth statement’s thicker scoring, try to keep hold of the repeated bass and drum rhythm. Adding players does not require replacing the simple underlying patterns.
cues.evidence: Statement 15 retains the score’s ostinato. Its start is estimated around 10:12 from the eighteen-bar sequence and changes around 10:05–10:15.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sixteenth statement: orchestral weight
cues.text: The sixteenth statement continues the second melody with expanded orchestral scoring. Follow its familiar phrase endings through the accumulated sound rather than expecting another tune.
cues.evidence: The score places the expanded second melody in statement 16. Its start is estimated around 10:52 from the eighteen-bar sequence and a rise in level around 10:45–10:50.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Seventeenth statement: first tune
cues.text: The seventeenth statement gives the first melody its last full appearance. Compare the massed scoring with the opening flute: orchestration has supplied most of the large-scale transformation.
cues.evidence: Statement 17 is the score’s last full first tune. Its start is estimated around 11:32 from the eighteen-bar sequence and a level rise around 11:25–11:30.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Eighteenth statement: second tune
cues.text: The eighteenth statement brings back the second melody in expanded orchestral scoring. Keep listening beneath it: the approaching break in the harmonic foundation will differ from another change of instrumental colour.
cues.evidence: Statement 18 precedes the score’s late modulation. Its start is estimated around 12:13 from the eighteen-bar sequence and the rise around 12:10–12:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The pattern finally breaks
cues.text: Near the end, eight bars in E major interrupt the long C-centred design. Listen for that harmonic departure as a different kind of change from the successive instrumental statements.
cues.evidence: The score specifies the eight-bar modulation. A strong measured change around 12:50 and E-major estimates around 12:55–13:00 support this approximate placement, not a precise chord onset.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return and abrupt ending
cues.text: The closing passage returns towards C and ends without a long diminuendo. Compare that abrupt ending with the gradual accumulation that occupied almost the whole piece.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the return to C. The report changes around 13:08 and drops from a high relative level around 13:15 to near silence by 13:20; individual attacks are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The melody changes hands, not its footing
transitions.how: Across the paired statements, Ravel keeps the eighteen-bar melodic span, the C-and-G bass foundation and the two-bar snare pattern running while the lead changes instrument. A closing phrase therefore does not stop the accompaniment or require a modulating bridge. Around this stage, solo colours give way to mixtures: horn, celesta and piccolos distribute the first melody across registers and related upper pitches. The seam is heard as a change in the body of the sound, not as a new tempo or tonic.
transitions.evidence: The Composite instruments boundary is 6:00; the report shows a relative-level rise around 5:55–6:00 without interruption of the recurring attack pattern. The score supplies the paired-statement method and ninth statement’s horn–celesta–piccolo mixture. The relations file corroborates an earlier flute-to-clarinet restatement, but neither it nor this timestamp identifies instruments from audio.

transitions.title: The bass finally abandons C
transitions.how: After almost the entire piece over the same C-centred foundation, Ravel shifts the full orchestral pattern to E major for eight bars. E–G♯–B replaces the familiar C-major harmonic ground: this is a direct tonal displacement, not another instrumental hand-over. The snare rhythm and triple metre continue, so the newly moving bass is heard against a mechanism that has not changed its gait. The long refusal to modulate makes this short departure carry disproportionate weight.
transitions.evidence: The E major boundary is 12:50, a strong novelty peak; local estimates around 12:55–13:00 are compatible with E major. The eight-bar departure, unchanged rhythmic pattern and written key come from the score, also described on the Ravel composer page. The audio feature supports passage placement, not an exactly identified first E-major chord.

transitions.title: C returns without another complete statement
transitions.how: The E-major excursion is forced back towards C, but Ravel does not restart an eighteen-bar melody. Trombone slides, percussion and dissonant orchestral attacks compress the remaining energy into the ending. The bass recovers the home centre while the repeated mechanism loses the space needed for another cycle. Instead of reversing the long crescendo with a diminuendo, the full orchestra terminates it with a short, forceful C-major close.
transitions.evidence: The C-major collapse boundary is 13:08, a strong novelty peak. Relative level remains high through 13:15 and is near silence at 13:20. The score supplies the return to C, trombone glissandi and compressed close; the report’s final minor-key estimates are not adopted as harmonic facts.

timeline.note: Snare rhythm above pizzicato violas and cellos; the melody has not begun.
Statement 1: solo flute, with snare drum and pizzicato lower strings.
Statement 2: clarinet takes the first tune; flute joins the rhythmic accompaniment.
Statement 3: high bassoon introduces the second tune; harp adds plucked chords.
Statement 4: E♭ clarinet repeats the second tune over flute rhythm and plucked accompaniment.
Statement 5: oboe d’amore restores the first tune; bassoons articulate the drum rhythm.
Statement 6: flute doubles muted trumpet an octave above; horn keeps the repeated rhythm.
Statement 7: tenor saxophone sings the second tune; muted trumpet supplies the rhythmic figure.
Statement 8: the higher saxophone line spans sopranino and soprano parts in the score.
Statement 9: horn, celesta and two piccolos combine the tune with its upper harmonics.
Statement 10: oboe, oboe d’amore, cor anglais and clarinets blend; inner strings add moving figures.
Statement 11: high solo trombone carries the second tune above bowed viola rhythm.
Statement 12: woodwinds and tenor saxophone share the second tune; second violins bow the ostinato.
Statement 13: divided first violins take the first tune with woodwinds; timpani reinforce the bass.
Statement 14: both violin sections join the first tune, doubled by winds and tenor saxophone.
Statement 15: trumpet reinforces the second tune with violins and upper winds; low brass supports.
Statement 16: trombones, soprano saxophone and strings broaden the second tune; horns maintain the rhythm.
Statement 17: first tune in upper winds, saxophones, trumpets and first violins; lower strings repeat chords.
Statement 18: solo trombone rejoins the massed second tune; lower strings drive the repeated accompaniment.
The massed melody shifts to E major while horns and lower strings retain the ostinato.
Trombone glissandi cut across the ostinato; cymbals, tam-tam and bass drum reinforce the collapse.

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
